title: Terraform module upgrade roadmap & publish checklist (private deployments)
content:
Purpose
This note captures a pragmatic, operations-friendly approach for versioning Terraform modules, publishing to our internal registry, and running breaking-change-safe upgrades for private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. It is intended for module authors, release engineers, and solutions engineers who onboard customers to Private.

Background and constraints
- Private deployments require strict compatibility guarantees: customers often pin module versions and upgrade on their schedule.
- We maintain a mix of provider versions (AWS, Azure), on-prem networking modules, and helper modules that interact with customer-managed resources.
- State migrations are expensive and customer-impactful; any change that touches resource identity (rename/type) must have an explicit migration plan.

Goals
1) Minimize customer surprise: clearly communicate breaking changes and provide migration helpers.
2) Maintain simple semantic versioning rules for modules tailored to Terraform semantics.
3) Automate registry publishing and release notes so rollouts are reproducible.
4) Provide a lightweight canary upgrade path and rollback guidance for private deployments.

Versioning rules (opinionated)
- Use a three-part version: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Map semantics to Terraform realities: 
  - PATCH (0.y.z -> 0.y.z+): bug fixes, docs, non-functional changes, provider pin updates that do not change resources. Safe to auto-apply.
  - MINOR (x.y+1.z): backward-compatible additions (new optional arguments with sensible defaults, new outputs, new module sub-resources that do not change existing resource addresses). Can be scheduled; recommend testing.
  - MAJOR (x+1.y.z): any change that renames/moves resources, changes resource types, changes required argument semantics, or removes outputs/arguments. Must follow breaking-change checklist and longer deprecation timeline.
- Pre-1.0 modules: treat MINOR as potentially breaking if we changed required semantics. Move to 1.0 when interface stabilizes and add migration notes for prior users.

Commit and PR conventions
- PR title prefix: [tf-module] <module-path>: short description
- Include a `version-bump` label and the target semver in the body.
- PR template must include: list of changed resource addresses, whether any resource addresses were renamed, schema changes to variables/outputs, and a link to a migration plan if applicable.

Registry publishing workflow (CI-driven)
1) Author opens PR to the module repo. Include changelog fragment under docs/changelog/unreleased/<version>.md describing intent and migration steps.
2) Automated CI runs: fmt, validate, `terraform init` + `terraform plan` against a standardized test harness for all supported provider versions.
3) If tests pass and reviewers sign off, maintainer runs release job (or CI with maintainer token) that:
   - runs `semantic-release`-style logic based on labels to pick semver,
   - builds a release archive,
   - tags the repo with vX.Y.Z,
   - pushes release artifacts to our private module registry along with metadata (supported providers, tested TF versions, changelog).
4) Post-publish steps: create release note in the internal releases doc and update the module index in the Private deployment docs. Notify solutions-engineering Slack channel and customers on the module watchlist.

Publish checklist (pre-release) — must be complete before MAJOR release
- [ ] Changelog entry in docs/changelog/unreleased
- [ ] PR includes explicit list of resource address changes and explanation
- [ ] Automated tests pass for all supported provider versions (matrix)
- [ ] Migration helper scripts (terraform import scripts, state mv examples) prepared and verified in sandbox
- [ ] Migration runbook drafted (including estimated downtime, manual steps, DB/state exports if applicable)
- [ ] Deprecation warnings added to module README for 30/60/90-day timeline if removing args/outputs
- [ ] Confluence migration page linked in PR and release note
- [ ] Customer-impact assessment completed (list of customers pinned to older versions)

Breaking-change checklist (detailed)
1) Confirm breaking nature: categorize change as rename/resource type change/required var change/output removal.
2) Draft migration strategy: re-addressing resources vs in-place changes via `terraform state mv`/`import`. Provide exact CLI commands and example `tfstate` snippet.
3) Prepare and test an end-to-end sandbox migration with a snapshot of state; include timing and failure-mode tests.
4) Add deprecation warnings in README & module outputs that detect old usage (where possible) and emit guidance.
5) Publish migration helpers in a dedicated folder: examples/migrations/vX.Y.Z/ with step-by-step checklist and idempotent scripts.
6) Coordinate customer rollout: owners list, support hours, and a rollback plan.
7) Lock down the release window and perform maintenance with solutions-engineering/SEs oncall.

Upgrade plan for downstream private deployments
- Canary stage: roll the module to a single non-critical tenant or an internal staging cluster using the new version. Test core flows and observe logs/metrics for 48 hours.
- Staging stage: after canary success, apply to an internal staging mirror of a customer or a non-prod customer. Run `terraform plan` with the new module and confirm no destructive diffs.
- Customer pilot: coordinate with 1–2 customers for guided upgrade, offer live support during operation window.
- General availability: after pilot confirms, announce GA and publish migration docs. Allow 90 days before removing deprecated args/outputs.

Automation & tests to reduce human risk
- Add a `compat` suite in CI that does: generate sample root modules for common patterns (vpc + dedicated GPU pool + ingress) and runs `terraform plan` with both old and new module versions to detect address changes and plan diffs.
- Maintain a small matrix of TF/core provider versions (latest minor + one previous minor) to avoid regressions from provider updates.
- Use `terratest` and lightweight containerized infra (localstack, kind, azurite) for provider-agnostic checks where possible.

Communication and deprecation cadence
- Minor changes: note in changelog and weekly module digest; no forced action.
- Major changes: 90-day deprecation window by default. Announce at day 0, 30, 60, 90 with example migration steps. Offer add-on migration engagement for enterprise customers.

Rollbacks and emergency handling
- If a release causes unexpected drift or resource recreation risk:
  1) Pause further rollouts.
  2) For customers who already applied the upgrade, provide `terraform state mv`/`import` steps or a fallback module alias that maps old addresses to new ones.
  3) If an automated rollback is required, maintain a 'previous' module registry alias (e.g., module-name@previous) and a documented path to re-point root modules and run `terraform apply` to return to the prior state.

Example changelog fragment (docs/changelog/unreleased/1.2.0.md)
- 1.2.0 (2025-06-18) — MINOR
  - Added optional `secondary_subnet_ids` for customer-managed HA setups (no impact when omitted).
  - Added `compatibility_notes.md` with migration examples.

Quick reference: actions for module author on a breaking change
- Draft migration plan + examples -> Add migration helper assets -> Add CHANGELOG + deprecation notes -> Run compat test matrix -> Open PR with `version-bump` label -> Post-merge, coordinate release job and customer notifications.

Open questions and follow-ups
- Should we provide automated `tfstate` transform tooling as part of release artifacts? (Pros: reduces manual work; Cons: risky to run blindly on customer state)
- Decide on default deprecation window for enterprise customers vs self-serve users (90 vs 180 days).

Appendix: sample state mv snippet
- terraform state mv module.old_module.aws_instance.worker[0] module.new_module.aws_instance.worker[0]

Notes to self
- Align with SEs to build a simple upgrade playbook template that can be copy/pasted per-customer.
- Add a short internal training session for on-call to walk through an example major upgrade.

End of document
